title: {{NAME}} and the Horn That Remembered Dinosaurs
moral: History is most alive in the things that remember it.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a sage-green royal tunic with silver and bone-white trim, dark trousers, and sage boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The unicorn's horn, when {{NAME}} first saw it, was different from others he'd read about: where most were pure silver or gold, this one had a banded quality, as if it contained layers, like rock strata.

The palace scholar said: "She carries old light. Light from before the first recorded history. Nobody knows quite what it means."

Princess Rosalind said: "She won't let most people near her horn. She let you near immediately."

{{NAME}} looked at the unicorn. The unicorn looked back.

"May I?" he asked.

She lowered her horn to him.

pages.content:
When he touched it, he saw: a landscape so ancient it had no name. Trees thirty metres tall. A sky with a different quality of blue.

And in that landscape: dinosaurs. Not distantly or impressionistically. Clearly, exactly, in motion, breathing.

He understood: the horn carried the visual memory of the time before the time before. Strata of history, each band a different era.

He touched the horn for thirty seconds. When he stepped back he could describe six species he had never studied.

"She was there," he said quietly. "Or something in her lineage was there."

pages.content:
The princess had been trying to identify a set of footprints found in the old quarry: too large for anything in current records, too distinctive to ignore.

{{NAME}} described the creatures from the horn's memory with as much detail as he could. The scholar cross-referenced them.

The footprints matched a species he had just seen in his vision: an Velociraptor variant, slightly larger than recorded specimens, from this specific region.

"There was a local population here," said the scholar, reading the match. "We didn't know."

"She knew," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
The discovery was published in the Royal Natural History journal.

The unicorn was credited as a primary source, which the editor had initially refused and then reconsidered when presented with the undeniable match between the horn-memory description and the fossil record.

"How do you credit a unicorn as a source?" the editor asked.

"Oral tradition," said {{NAME}}. "Exceptionally old."

Princess Rosalind signed the paper. {{NAME}} signed it. The scholar signed it.

The unicorn, when the published copy was read aloud to her, lowered her horn once: acknowledged.

pages.content:
He walked home thinking about the vision in the horn: that ancient landscape with a different sky.

The information had been there all along. It had just needed someone to ask and someone else who was willing to remember.

In his room, he took out his sketchbook and drew from memory: the ancient forest, the quality of the light, the Velociraptor variant as he'd seen it.

He worked until his eyes were heavy.

He left the sketchbook open and fell asleep, and in his dreams the landscape was still there, green and ancient and alive.
